name: Wôpanâak

catalog_locator: preprint p. 2, §1 'Wôpanâak background', rule (1); restated verbatim as (65) in §2.7 Summary, p. 49; final syllables p. 37; primary vs secondary stress p. 47 (§2.5.2 pp. 38-47); mata exception pp. 17-18; no consonant-cluster weight pp. 24-25; word-level stress p. 25; skippable schwa §3 pp. 50-56; conclusion p. 56.
catalog_quote: Stress in Wôpanâak, I will argue, is governed by rules very similar to those of Lenape (Delaware: Goddard 1979, 2021, Hayes 1995). In particular: (1) a. Long vowels are stressed. b. In sequences of syllables with short vowels, the even-numbered vowels are stressed. c. The last syllable of a word is not stressed, unless this is the only stress in the word. d. Main stress goes on the last stressed syllable of the word. One general exception to these rules is the word mata 'no, not' which receives initial stress; I discuss this case in section 2.2 below. In section 3 I will turn to another kind of exception; we will see there that certain instances of unstressed schwa are skipped by the stress rule in (1b), allowing for multiple unstressed vowels between stresses. [p. 2] ... I have also proposed that of the stressed syllables, the primary stress is on the last non-final stress; this is why this is the stress which is preferentially aligned with iambic beats in words with only two stresses. [p. 47] ... Lenape short vowels followed by consonant clusters may be reliably stressed, but in Wôpanâak they are not [p. 25]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Every long vowel (â, ee, 8, ô) is stressed; among runs of short-vowel syllables (a, u=schwa), counting from the word beginning or from the last long vowel, the even-numbered (2nd, 4th..) syllables are stressed (an iambic alternation); a word-final syllable is never stressed unless it would be the word's only stress; primary stress falls on the rightmost (non-final) stressed syllable, earlier stresses being secondary. Unlike Lenape, a short vowel before a consonant cluster is not thereby stressed (p. 20-21). Certain reliably unstressed schwas are skipped when counting (§3, pp. 49-55).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: all syllables meeting (1a-b) carry stress; 'the primary stress is on the last non-final stress' and earlier ones are secondary (§2.5.2, pp. 33-46, e.g. <waantog> with secondary stress on syllable 1 and primary on 2; 'main stress on the fourth syllable and secondary stress on the second' in ex. (68), p. 50).
new_statements.exceptions: mata 'no, not' takes initial stress (possibly underlyingly umata) (§2.2, pp. 16-17); certain instances of unstressed schwa (e.g. the schwa after â in the final -ânutam, and epenthetic schwa before -hutut) are 'skipped' for purposes of counting short vowels, allowing several unstressed vowels between stresses (§3); six unexplained 'mysteries' remain in the Psalms data (p. 31).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress of an extinct 17th-18th-century language, reconstructed (not observed) mainly from the alignment of words with iambic beats in Eliot's metrical Psalms (1663/1685) plus patterns of short-vowel loss in the wider corpus; no instrumental or speaker data exist. The author notes the rules are used by the Wôpanâak Language Reclamation Project's revived variety. Eliot 1666 pp. 2-3 (open, downloaded) gives only 'Anum [um produced]' and an acute accent 'to shew which Syllable is first produced', used only sometimes.
new_statements.identity_note: Wôpanâak = Wampanoag = Massachusett = Natick (Glottolog wamp1249, ISO wam). Richards describes the 17th-18th-century written language, principally the Natick-based literary variety of Eliot's Bible and metrical Psalms (Massachusett proper), and the stress system now taught in the Wôpanâak Language Reclamation Project's revived variety; the rules are reconstructed from texts, not from speakers. No dialect-level glottocode applies.

sources.note: Full reconstruction of the stress system from the metrical Psalms and vowel-loss patterns: long vowels stressed; in short-vowel sequences even-numbered vowels stressed; final syllable unstressed unless sole stress; main stress on last stressed syllable; mata 'not' exceptionally initial; some unstressed schwas skipped in the count (section 3).

tone.quote: Unstressed Mass /ə/ (as determined by a rhythmic stress pattern similar to that of other Algonquian languages) is subject to being dropped, apparently optionally; the resulting clusters are sometimes simplified orthographically, with plain (n) written for presumed [nn] as the realization of /nən/, for example: ukkeninuh, ukkinuh 'he carries, embraces him, them', ukkinunnóuh, ukkinóuh 'they carry him, them' (T 33; Gen. 33:4)
tone.locator: p. 68, §29 (PA *e > PEA *ə > Mass /ə/); the work contains no tone passage, this is its only statement on word prosody
